A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same JDR research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original cSBM and real-graph experiments, component and hyperparameter ablations, spectral-clustering results, and Gaussian-model simulations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds benchmark, scalability, FoSR-comparison and alignment results.

M1.justification: The decomposition, sign-corrected eigenvector interpolation, iterative synthesis and final update procedure remain unchanged. Appendix Algorithm 1 is identical apart from spacing. The new formal analysis and truncated-decomposition discussion do not establish a changed JDR algorithm.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained cSBM and ten original benchmarks, v2 evaluates Roman-empire, Amazon-ratings, Minesweeper, Tolokers, Questions, Penn94 and Twitch-gamers (Tables 4 and 7). Coverage expands to a game-grid task and larger user/social networks, reaching 168,114 nodes.

E2.justification: FoSR, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator across the retained GCN/GPRGNN benchmark settings and spectral-clustering comparisons. This adds a directly relevant spectral-rewiring alternative throughout the evaluation. DIGL was already evaluated in v1's appendix; its appearance in v2's main tables is retained evidence.

E3.justification: The added benchmarks introduce source-provided splits, ROC AUC for imbalanced Minesweeper, Tolokers and Questions, and dedicated large-graph model configurations. Table 15 specifies five-layer GCN with residuals for Questions and four-layer GCN for Twitch-gamers. The original sparse/dense protocols and settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a focused extension of the alignment analysis: DIGL comparisons on cSBM and comparisons among rewiring methods across the original real graphs (Appendix A.5.4, Figures 7–8). The existing component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity/transfer studies and Gaussian-MSE analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The general practice remains 100 random-split runs with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 1,000 resamples; Gaussian simulations retain ten trials and standard-deviation bands. v2 additionally specifies ten splits for the new Twitch-gamers experiment in Appendix A.8. This does not establish changed run counts for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial results for new datasets, FoSR and alignment analyses. Newly reported Penn94 accuracy is 82.30% for GCN+JDR versus 80.40% for GCN (Table 4). FoSR also becomes the highest reported mean on dense-split PubMed with GPRGNN: 89.28% versus the unchanged JDR score of 89.24% (Table 8).

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 1 and its Appendix A.3 proof of asymptotic one-step label-alignment improvement under independent GOE noise, lambda > sqrt(2), and sufficiently small interpolation. It also supplies a rotational-invariance proof, a computational-complexity derivation and explicit norm bounds in Equation 4. v1's earlier random-matrix discussion remains.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add theoretical justification as a central contribution: JDR improves label alignment under a stylized GOE model, with extension to cSBM suggested conjecturally. v1 principally presents a heuristic with empirical support and leaves theoretical guarantees open. v2 also explicitly frames its comparisons around preprocessing rewiring.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive boundaries concerning graph-level tasks, strong adversarial perturbations, million-node scalability and Minesweeper's failure case. Its alignment discussion explains why improved accuracy need not accompany increased alignment for other methods. The earlier nonlinear-feature limitation is retained in Appendix A.2, rather than removed.

D1.justification: v2 extends the existing detailed documentation with large-graph configurations, FoSR iteration counts and resource disclosures, including roughly 60 minutes and 500 GB of memory for Twitch-gamers. Code access remains unchanged. Conversely, v1's explicit final feature-blending equation is replaced by a brief interpolation description.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to distinguish preprocessing from end-to-end rewiring and discuss graph transformers, regularization and additional cSBM research. New works include Gutteridge et al., Qian et al. and Ando and Zhang. JDR's positioning relative to adversarial graph structure learning is also substantially clarified.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution statement are substantially rewritten. Related work moves from before the method to after the experiments and gains topic-based organization; the low-dimensional resonance discussion moves to the appendix. The appendices are reorganized, and citations change from numbered to author–year style.

P2.justification: v2 adds a method-comparison table, large-graph and additional heterophilic result tables, and alignment plots. Existing benchmark and hyperparameter tables gain rows or columns, while DIGL results are also displayed in the main text. Existing figures are resized or relocated, and the principal cSBM performance plot gains labeled regime shading.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the justification and validation of JDR: the restricted GOE proof adds formal support, FoSR supplies a directly relevant missing comparison, and broader benchmarks test practical scope beyond v1's evaluation. Comparative alignment evidence and explicit failure conditions improve interpretation. The guarantee remains narrow and the final feature-blending update becomes less explicit, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and clarity about applicability.
